name: Thymosin Beta-4
lead: Thymosin beta-4 (Tβ4) is a small, abundant peptide of about 43 amino acids, encoded by the TMSB4X gene, whose best-established role is binding monomeric actin and thereby regulating the cell cytoskeleton [1][2][3]. It was first isolated from calf thymus and sequenced in 1981 by the group of Allan Goldstein [4].

Outside cells it has been reported to promote cell migration, blood-vessel formation and tissue repair [1]. Phase 2 trials have tested it in skin ulcers, epidermolysis bullosa, dry eye and corneal wounds, and cardiac trials were registered [5][6][7][8]. In looksmaxxing and recovery communities it is discussed mainly as a hair-growth and healing "research peptide", with a related fragment sold as TB-500. Hair findings come from mouse studies, and no approved use exists [2].

paras: Tβ4 binds G-actin in a 1:1 complex and keeps a pool of unpolymerized actin available, a function worked out in cell-biology studies of profilin and actin dynamics [9][10]. Additional extracellular signaling roles are reported but not fully defined [1].

Phase 2 trials reported by sponsors include pressure ulcers (72 participants), venous stasis ulcers (72), epidermolysis bullosa (30, terminated), corneal wounds in diabetes (12, terminated) and dry eye (72) [5][6][7][8][11][12]. Reviews summarized by Wikipedia describe faster wound repair and good tolerability in the wound trials, and improvement in dry eye and neurotrophic keratopathy [2]. Grokipedia states that the venous ulcer results were not conclusively better than placebo and that a 2025 Phase 3 trial of an ophthalmic formulation missed its primary endpoint [13].

Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers were completed [14][15], and two cardiac trials in myocardial infarction were withdrawn, with a new Phase 2 registered for 2026 [16][17][18]. No trial of hair growth in people was found.

Researchers studying wound healing observed faster hair growth near wound edges and then reported that Tβ4 accelerated hair growth in healthy mice, with follicle stem cell activation described [2][13]. These models used normal hair cycling; no reliable evidence for alopecia was found [13].

Trials reported mild effects and no serious adverse events, but long-term data are lacking [13]. Because the peptide promotes blood-vessel growth and has been linked to tumor metastasis in cancer research, tumor promotion is described as a theoretical concern, with no causal link shown in human trials [13]. Products sold outside regulated channels may vary in purity [13].

The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits Tβ4 and derivatives such as TB-500 [2][13]. Its use attracted attention in Australian sport in the 2010s, notably the Cronulla Sharks and Essendon cases, with a 2016 Court of Arbitration for Sport award in the Essendon matter [2]. It has no FDA or EMA approval and is sold online as a research product [13].

timeline.event: Thymosin fraction 5 prepared from calf thymus by Goldstein's group, the source from which Tβ4 was later purified.[13]
Complete amino acid sequence of bovine Tβ4 published.[4]

card.summary: A natural actin-binding peptide with wound and eye trials and mouse hair data; sold as TB-500, banned in sport.
card.note: Not approved; no human hair trials; WADA-prohibited.

quick.overview:
Thymosin beta-4 is a naturally occurring 43-amino-acid peptide that regulates actin in cells. Phase 2 trials tested it for skin ulcers and eye conditions, with mixed or incomplete results reported.

Hair-growth claims rest on mouse studies. It circulates online as a research peptide, along with the fragment TB-500.
quick.mechanism: It binds monomeric actin to control cell structure and movement, and is reported to promote cell migration and new blood vessels outside cells.
quick.risks: Trials reported mild effects, but long-term data are lacking. Its blood-vessel-promoting activity raises theoretical tumor concerns. It is unapproved, WADA-prohibited, and gray-market products vary in purity.
